body.heading: A field that feels fingers
paragraphs: Most modern touchscreens are capacitive. Beneath the glass lies a transparent grid of electrodes holding a tiny electrical charge, creating a faint electrostatic field at the surface. Your body conducts electricity, so when a finger touches the glass it steals a minute amount of charge at that spot.

Circuits at the edges measure exactly how much charge each row and column lost, and from those changes the controller calculates the touch point — often tracking ten fingers at once, many times a second, for pinches, swipes and two-handed typing.

body.heading: Why gloves defeat it
paragraphs: The system relies on your finger's conductivity. An ordinary glove insulates the finger, the charge theft stops, and the screen sees nothing — which is why special gloves have conductive thread woven into the fingertips. A stylus with a soft conductive tip works for the same reason: it couples your body's charge through to the glass, while a plain plastic pen, electrically invisible, does nothing at all.

Older resistive screens worked differently, by pressure: two flexible layers were pushed into contact. They responded to any stylus or gloved hand but needed a firmer press and dulled the display — one reason capacitive glass took over on phones.

body.heading: Glass that only pretends to be simple
paragraphs: The sensing grid is made from indium tin oxide, a material that is both electrically conductive and nearly transparent — a rare combination that lets the screen watch your fingers without blocking the picture beneath.

Water confuses the system, since droplets conduct too; phone software works hard to tell raindrops and wet palms from real touches. The screen you tap so casually is solving a small electrical puzzle with every contact.

description: Most touchscreens sense your finger electrically: your body disturbs a faint field, and the screen spots where.
